snip.t: Ischaemic stroke – sudden neurological deficit lasting >24 h (or until death) caused by an acute interruption of cerebral blood flow due to arterial occlusion.
Combined hormonal contraception is generally contraindicated in migraine with aura due to elevated ischaemic stroke risk.
Thromboembolic: Ischaemic stroke, mesenteric ischaemia, acute limb ischaemia (primarily from AF).
Systemic and Pulmonary Thromboembolism: Mural thrombus dislodgement causes ischaemic stroke, renal infarction, or limb ischaemia; deep vein thromboses lead to pulmonary embolism.

faq.a: Reperfusion with thrombolysis is not recommended, but thrombectomy may be possible up to 24 h for large‑vessel occlusion if imaging shows salvageable tissue.
faq.q: Can a stroke be treated after 4.5 hours?

faq.a: Lowering perfusion pressure can worsen the infarct; only treat if >220/120 mmHg or before thrombolysis.
faq.q: Why is blood pressure not lowered aggressively in acute ischaemic stroke?

faq.a: If cardio‑embolic source is confirmed, start after 1‑2 weeks once haemorrhagic transformation risk is low.
faq.q: When should anticoagulation be started after an ischaemic stroke?

exam: A 58‑year‑old with sudden right‑sided weakness arrives 3 h after symptom onset – what is the next step and why? — Assess BP, obtain non‑contrast CT, if no bleed and BP <185/110 give IV alteplase.
How does atrial fibrillation change secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke? — Requires lifelong anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet alone.
What imaging finding distinguishes a large‑vessel occlusion suitable for thrombectomy? — CTA/MRA shows occlusion of ICA or M1 segment with a small core infarct on perfusion maps.
Why is aspirin started after 24 h rather than immediately in a patient who received thrombolysis? — To reduce re‑bleeding risk; antiplatelet added once haemostasis is assured.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with acute focal deficit – how does management differ? — Prioritise rapid transfusion to reduce HbS, consider exchange transfusion before thrombolysis if feasible.
What red‑flag sign would make you postpone thrombolysis despite a short onset time? — Blood pressure >185/110 mmHg, active bleeding, or recent major surgery.
Explain why a normal early CT does not exclude ischaemic stroke. — Early cytotoxic oedema may be invisible; clinical picture and later MRI confirm diagnosis.

How would you differentiate a stroke from a severe migraine aura in a low‑resource setting? — Migraine lacks persistent motor weakness and imaging remains normal; stroke shows focal deficit lasting >24 h.
ai.title: Ischaemic Stroke
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sudden focal neurological deficit caused by arterial occlusion of brain tissue. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and imaging; management prioritises reperfusion, secondary prevention and addressing local risk factors.

b: Clinical diagnosis: focal deficit with rapid onset
Imaging: non‑contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage; CT‑angiography or MRI if available
sections.p: An ischaemic stroke is a sudden neurological deficit lasting more than 24 h (or until death) due to acute interruption of cerebral blood flow by arterial occlusion.

b: NIHSS guides thrombolysis eligibility and prognosis
CT perfusion or MRI diffusion‑perfusion mismatch identifies salvageable tissue
sections.p: Severity is graded with the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS); scores 0‑4 mild, 5‑15 moderate, 16‑20 moderate‑severe, >20 severe. Early imaging classifies tissue as core infarct vs penumbra.

b: Cardio‑embolism (atrial fibrillation, rheumatic mitral stenosis, endocarditis, HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy)
Large‑artery atherosclerosis (carotid plaque, hypertension, diabetes)
Small‑vessel disease (lacunes, hypertension, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion)
Other: vasculitis, malaria‑related cerebral sequestration, sickle‑cell crisis, drug‑induced vasospasm
sections.p: Most strokes are thrombo‑embolic. In low‑resource settings, additional contributors include infectious and rheumatic heart disease‑related emboli.

b: Face‑arm‑speech test positive for unilateral facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech
Sudden visual field cut (homonymous hemianopia)
Acute confusion or decreased level of consciousness if brainstem involved
sections.p: Patients present with abrupt onset of focal deficits: unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, visual field loss, or altered consciousness.

t.b: Is the deficit haemorrhagic? – Shows hyperdense bleed; normal or early ischaemia supports thrombolysis
Is there a large‑vessel occlusion? – Demonstrates clot location; guides thrombectomy
Is hypoglycaemia mimicking stroke? – <3.0 mmol/L suggests metabolic cause; treat glucose first
Is infection or inflammatory vasculitis present? – Elevated markers may point to TB meningitis or HIV vasculopathy
Is cardio‑embolism likely? – A‑fib or arrhythmia detected; prompts anticoagulation
Is carotid stenosis the source? – >70 % stenosis may need endarterectomy
Rely on clinical NIHSS, blood glucose, and bedside assessment; consider transfer if thrombolysis possible

b: Rapid neurological decline – suggests expanding infarct or haemorrhagic transformation
Severe hypertension >220/120 mmHg – risk of bleed if thrombolysis planned
Airway compromise in brainstem stroke
Deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism from immobility
sections.p: Early complications can be fatal and require urgent action.

b: IV alteplase within 4.5 h if onset known, BP <185/110, no contraindications
Mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 h for large‑vessel occlusion when resources allow
Anticoagulation (warfarin or DOAC) for cardio‑embolic sources; avoid in recent bleed
Control glucose, temperature, and treat seizures if present
Physiotherapy and early mobilisation to prevent DVT and pressure sores
sections.p: Reperfusion, secondary prevention and supportive care are the pillars.

b: Blood pressure target <130/80 mmHg; use ACE‑inhibitor or thiazide if affordable
Statin for all patients regardless of cholesterol level
Screen for atrial fibrillation; consider anticoagulation if present
Treat HIV, TB, sickle‑cell disease aggressively to lower stroke risk
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet low in salt, regular exercise
sections.p: Long‑term risk reduction focuses on modifiable vascular factors and addressing local disease burdens.

b: Transient ischaemic attack – deficit resolves <24 h, no infarction on imaging
Intracerebral haemorrhage – hyperdense bleed on CT, contraindicates thrombolysis
Migraine aura – visual symptoms without focal weakness, normal imaging
Early CT may appear normal despite infarction – do not rule out stroke
Blood glucose extremes can mimic or mask deficits – always check
Mild carotid stenosis on Doppler may be underestimated without angiography

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of weakness, speech loss or visual loss
Severe headache with vomiting after a focal deficit
